question: Can a resistor draw a current whose fundamental lags the voltage, leads it, or lines up exactly? <silence msec='550'/> Here, the same two gate turn-off thyristors control the same twelve-ohm resistor. In all three cases, the load receives exactly ten Joules per cycle. The only thing we change is when the switches conduct.
energy: The source supplies one hundred twenty volts R M S at sixty hertz. Each half-cycle must deliver five Joules. The shaded area comes from integrating resistor power over time. Where the voltage is high, a narrow window is enough. As the window moves away from the peak, it must widen to keep the energy fixed.
unity: Start with the window centered at ninety degrees. The left panel shows the resistor power. On the right, the voltage sets the horizontal reference for the fundamental current phasor. The current points straight to the right: five Amperes in phase, zero in quadrature. The source supplies no fundamental reactive power.
lag: Now delay the positive gate. Watch its turn-off edge move out as well. The shaded area still represents five Joules. The tip of the current phasor moves downward along the five-Ampere line. At thirty degrees of lag, the source supplies about three hundred forty-six Volt-Amperes reactive. The in-phase current is still five Amperes.
lead: Sweep the window back through the centered case and toward the beginning of the half-cycle. Watch the phasor cross the horizontal axis. At thirty degrees of lead it points upward, and fundamental reactive power changes sign. The early and late windows have exactly the same width. They are reflections of each other about the voltage peak.
gates: These are the gate commands, measured from the rising voltage zero crossing. The second G T O repeats the first command one hundred eighty degrees later. Each colored interval is a gate-on command. The leading case puts most of the current pulse before the voltage peak. The lagging case puts most of it after the peak.
mirror: Reflecting a current pulse in time changes its harmonic phases while preserving each harmonic magnitude. Look at the three colored bars for each order. The leading and lagging cases match at every order. Their current distortion is about seventy-one percent. The centered window gives one hundred percent. All three waveforms have zero direct current and zero even harmonics.
fourier: Watch the Fourier sums build all three currents. The dashed traces show the ideal switch currents. Begin with zero direct current, then add the fundamental. Each odd order changes the shape of the pulse. After order nine, we speed up to order fifty. Notice how the ripples at the edges of the leading and lagging pulses mirror each other.
result: Ten Joules per cycle at sixty hertz fixes the active power at six hundred watts. For the same resistor, that also fixes total R M S current at seven point zero seven Amperes. The true power factor is therefore point seven zero seven in all three cases. The sign of fundamental reactive power follows the timing of the current. The resistor still absorbs energy whenever it conducts.
